course_title: Biology for Health Sciences Part B

learning_outcomes.description: Identify and explain the structure and function of the cardiovascular, respiratory, digestive, renal, and integumentary systems
Identify and explain the structure and function of the reproductive system and the principles of human development
Describe how homeostatic mechanisms regulate the function of the human body through multiple systems
Differentiate between innate and acquired immunity, and describe the role of immunology in medicine
Explain the structure and function of the components of microbial cells and how pathogenic microbes cause disease
Display sound scientific reasoning in the context of practical sessions in human anatomy, human physiology, immunology and microbiology
Apply critical thinking and reasoning skills to understand and analyse the interconnectedness and interdependencies of various biological systems studied to date.
Effectively communicate complex anatomical and physiological concepts orally and/or in written form to various audiences.

assessments.task_description:
To enhance your understanding of course content, eleven (11) content-specific workshops will be offered throughout the semester. In each workshop, you must complete a specified assessment activity and submit it before departure. You will earn 5% toward your final course grade if you complete and submit at least eight (8) of these eleven (11) activities.

Please note: completing fewer than eight (8) activities will result in a 0% for this component.

Further assessment details will be provided on Blackboard during the semester.

We recommend that you do not use the Blackboard Phone App nor a wireless network connection when completing this Blackboard assessment. Both are unstable and could affect your ability to complete your Blackboard assessment, by for example:

  • you may lose connectivity and lose the work you have completed;
  • your submission could indicate you have completed your assessment task, but nothing has been delivered into BlackBoard.

Please ensure that you only use a reliable internet connection.

Missed Workshops?

You have been given ample notice to manage your schedule and attend the required sessions. However, if you are unable to attend due to illness or exceptional circumstances, please contact your Course Coordinator promptly to discuss alternative arrangements.

Academic Integrity Notice

This task has been designed to be challenging, authentic and complex. Whilst students may use AI and/or MT technologies, successful completion of assessment in this course will require students to critically engage in specific contexts and tasks for which artificial intelligence will provide only limited support and guidance. A failure to reference generative AI or MT use may constitute student misconduct under the Student Code of Conduct. To pass this assessment, students will be required to demonstrate detailed comprehension of their written submission independent of AI and MT tools.

learning_activities.topic:
Lecture series - Respiratory System by Dr Danielle Burgess

BIOM1071- Respiratory System Module

Lecturer: Dr Danielle Burgess

Contact Hours: 5 lectures

Module Overview

In this module, you will explore the structure and function of the respiratory system. The content is organised into five key areas:

1. Anatomy of the Respiratory System

  • Identify the major anatomical structures.
  • Distinguish between the upper and lower respiratory tracts in terms of structure and function.

2. Mechanics of Breathing

  • Understand how the components of the thoracic cavity work together.
  • Explain the role of pressure changes (intrapulmonary, intrapleural, and atmospheric) in driving inspiration and expiration.

3. Gas Transport and Homeostasis

  • Learn how the body regulates oxygen (O₂) and carbon dioxide (CO₂) levels to maintain acid–base balance.
  • Describe the physiological mechanisms that keep blood gases within normal ranges.

4. Gas Exchange

  • Understand the principles of diffusion at the alveoli- capillary interface.
  • Explain the importance of gas exchange for cellular metabolism and overall body function.

5. Measuring Respiratory Function

  • Receive a brief introduction to common pulmonary function tests (e.g., spirometry).
  • Key concepts will be reinforced and applied during practical classes- attendance and participation are encouraged.

Learning Outcomes

By the end of this module, you should be able to:

  • Describe the anatomy and divisions of the respiratory system.
  • Explain the physical and pressure-based events underlying breathing.
  • Discuss how O₂ and CO₂ are transported and regulated.
  • Outline the process and significance of gas exchange.
  • Interpret basic respiratory measurements.


Preparation

Review lecture slides before each session and bring any questions to class. Practical sessions will build on these concepts, so active engagement is advised.


Learning outcomes: L01, L03, L06, L07, L08

learning_activities.topic:
Introduction to BIOM1071 by Dr Awais Saleem Babri

The BIOM1071 introductory lecture serves as the academic roadmap for the semester, establishing the foundational framework for human anatomy and physiology. It will begin with a formal welcome, covering administrative essentials such as the course outline, assessment schedule, hurdle requirements, and key academic integrity policies. Academically, the lecture will introduce the core theme of "structure meeting function," bridging microscopic cellular biology with macroscopic organ systems. The course coordinator will define the specific anatomical terminology and directional planes required for describing the human body, while explaining the core physiological principles of homeostasis and negative feedback loops that underpin all bodily regulation. Importantly, the session will set clear expectations for the intensive practical laboratory component, outlining safety protocols, group work dynamics, and proper use of facilities and equipment. Finally, it will provide a brief preview of the upcoming weekly modules, offering students practical guidance on efficient study strategies, recommended resources and how to access academic support services. The overarching goal is to ensure every student is prepared, motivated, and fully aware of what is required to succeed in this foundational course.

learning_activities.topic:
Lecture series - Cardiovascular System by Dr Niwanthi Rajapakse

BIOM1071- Cardiovascular System Module

Lecturer: Dr Niwanthi Rajapakse

Contact Hours: 5 lectures + 1 revision lecture

Module Overview

In this module, you will examine the structure and function of the cardiovascular system and its associated fluid—blood. The content is organised into five key areas:

1. Anatomy of the Cardiovascular System

  • Identify the major anatomical structures of the heart and blood vessels.
  • Describe how each region (chambers, valves, and vessel types) contributes to the direction and maintenance of blood flow.

2. Blood Composition and Function

  • Understand the components of blood (plasma, red cells, white cells, platelets).
  • Explain the roles of blood in transport, defence, and homeostasis.

3. The Cardiac Cycle

  • Learn the sequence of events in one complete heartbeat.
  • Distinguish between systole (contraction) and diastole (relaxation) in each chamber.

4. Cardiac Output and Blood Pressure

  • Define cardiac output (heart rate × stroke volume) and its determinants.
  • Explore the factors that influence mean arterial pressure (MAP), including peripheral resistance and blood volume.

5. Electrical Properties of the Heart

  • Understand the origin and pathway of the cardiac action potential.
  • Describe the role of the conducting system (SA node, AV node, bundle branches, Purkinje fibres) in coordinating rhythmic contraction.
  • Relate electrical activity to the ECG (electrocardiogram) and its clinical relevance.

Learning Outcomes

By the end of this module, you should be able to:

  • Describe the anatomy of the heart, blood vessels, and blood components.
  • Explain the events of the cardiac cycle and how they produce heart sounds.
  • Define cardiac output and identify factors that alter mean arterial pressure.
  • Outline the electrical conduction system and interpret basic ECG waveforms.
  • Integrate structure, function, and electrical activity to explain normal cardiovascular physiology.

Preparation

Review lecture materials before each session and bring any questions to class. Concepts from this module will connect with later topics in the course, so active engagement and note-taking are strongly recommended.


Learning outcomes: L01, L03, L06, L07, L08

learning_activities.topic:
Lecture series - Digestive & Renal system by Dr Judit Kibedi

BIOM1071- Digestive & Renal Systems Module

Lecturer: Dr Judit Kibedi

Contact Hours: 7 lectures

Module Overview

In this module, you will explore the anatomy and physiology of two interconnected systems, the digestive system and the renal (urinary) system, and examine how they work together to regulate nutrients, fluid balance, and waste elimination. The content is organised into four key areas:

1. Anatomy of the Digestive System

  • Identify the major organs and accessory structures of the gastrointestinal (GI) tract.
  • Trace the pathway of food from ingestion to egestion, noting the function of each region.

2. Physiology of Digestion and Nutrient Regulation

  • Understand the processes of mechanical and chemical digestion, including enzyme action and hormonal control.
  • Explain how nutrients are absorbed across the intestinal wall and distributed to the body.
  • Describe the role of the digestive system in maintaining overall metabolic homeostasis.

3. Anatomy of the Renal System

  • Identify the macroscopic structures of the kidneys, ureters, bladder, and urethra.
  • Focus on the nephron as the functional unit of the kidney—learn the specific regions (glomerulus, proximal tubule, loop of Henle, distal tubule, collecting duct).
  • Recognise the key cell types within the kidney and their roles in filtration, reabsorption, and secretion.

4. Renal Physiology and Homeostasis

  • Understand how the kidneys filter blood and produce urine.
  • Explain the mechanisms of reabsorption (returning water and solutes to the blood) and secretion (removing additional wastes).
  • Describe how the renal system regulates fluid volume, electrolyte balance, and acid–base balance to maintain homeostasis.
  • Connect renal function to long-term regulation of blood pressure and red blood cell production (erythropoietin).

Learning Outcomes

By the end of this module, you should be able to:

  • Describe the anatomy and primary functions of the digestive and renal systems.
  • Explain how nutrients are processed and absorbed, and how wastes are generated and eliminated.
  • Identify the regions of the nephron and relate each region to specific reabsorptive or secretory functions.
  • Discuss how the kidneys respond to changes in body fluid and solute levels to restore homeostasis.
  • Integrate digestive and renal functions to explain whole‑body nutrient and waste management.


Important Administrative Note

Lecture on 15th September: This session will be delivered online rather than in person. I will post information closer to the date

  • Further details (e.g., platform link, scheduled time, access instructions) will be provided via Announcements on Blackboard.
  • Please check Blackboard regularly leading up to this date to ensure you don't miss any updates.


Preparation

  • Review lecture slides and recommended readings before each session. These two systems are closely linked in physiology, making connections between them as you study will deepen your understanding. Active participation and note‑taking are encouraged throughout the module.

Learning outcomes: L01, L03, L06, L07, L08

learning_activities.topic:
Lecture series - Reproductive System by Dr Cassy Spiller

BIOM1071- Reproduction Module

Lecturer: Dr Cassy Spiller

Contact Hours: 4 lectures

Module Overview

In this module, you will explore the anatomy and physiology of the male and female reproductive systems, the process of fertilisation, and the key stages of human development. The content also includes important clinical applications relevant to reproductive health. The material is organised into five key areas:

1. Anatomy of the Male Reproductive Tract

  • Identify the major structures (testes, epididymis, vas deferens, accessory glands, penis).
  • Describe the function of each structure in sperm production, maturation, transport, and delivery.

2. Anatomy of the Female Reproductive Tract

  • Identify the major structures (ovaries, fallopian tubes, uterus, cervix, vagina).
  • Describe the function of each structure in oocyte production, fertilisation, implantation, and pregnancy support.

3. Physiology of Reproduction

  • Understand the hormonal regulation of the male reproductive cycle (hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis, testosterone production).
  • Understand the hormonal regulation of the female reproductive cycle (follicular phase, ovulation, luteal phase, and the roles of oestrogen and progesterone).
  • Explain the process of gametogenesis (spermatogenesis and oogenesis).

4. Fertilisation and Early Development

  • Trace the pathway of sperm from ejaculation to egg encounter.
  • Describe the events of fertilisation (sperm-egg fusion, cortical reaction, formation of the zygote).
  • Outline the early stages of embryonic development (cleavage, morula, blastocyst formation, implantation).
  • Introduce the formation of the germ layers and basic developmental milestones.

5. Clinical Aspects of Reproduction

  • Gain an overview of common reproductive health issues (e.g., infertility, contraceptive methods, sexually transmitted infections).
  • Understand the basis of assisted reproductive technologies (e.g., IVF).
  • Recognise how hormonal imbalances or anatomical abnormalities can affect fertility and pregnancy outcomes.


Learning Outcomes

By the end of this module, you should be able to:

  • Describe the anatomy and primary functions of the male and female reproductive tracts.
  • Explain the hormonal control of gamete production and the reproductive cycles.
  • Outline the process of fertilisation and the key events of early human development.
  • Identify common clinical conditions affecting reproduction and their physiological basis.
  • Integrate anatomical, physiological, and clinical knowledge to understand reproductive health.


Preparation

Review lecture materials before each session and bring any questions to class. This module includes clinically relevant content, active engagement will help you connect basic science to real‑world applications. Regular revision of hormonal pathways and anatomical diagrams is strongly recommended.



Learning outcomes: L02, L03, L06, L07, L08

Explain the process of gametogenesis (spermatogenesis and oogenesis). 4. Fertilisation and Early Development Trace the pathway of sperm from ejaculation to egg encounter. Describe the events of fertilisation (sperm-egg fusion, cortical reaction, formation of the zygote). Outline the early stages of embryonic development (cleavage, morula, blastocyst formation, implantation). Introduce the formation of the germ layers and basic developmental milestones. 5. Clinical Aspects of Reproduction Gain an overview of common reproductive health issues (e.g., infertility, contraceptive methods, sexually transmitted infections). Understand the basis of assisted reproductive technologies (e.g., IVF). Recognise how hormonal imbalances or anatomical abnormalities can affect fertility and pregnancy outcomes. Learning Outcomes By the end of this module, you should be able to: Describe the anatomy and primary functions of the male and female reproductive tracts. Explain the hormonal control of gamete production and the reproductive cycles. Outline the process of fertilisation and the key events of early human development. Identify common clinical conditions affecting reproduction and their physiological basis. Integrate anatomical, physiological, and clinical knowledge to understand reproductive health. Preparation Review lecture materials before each session and bring any questions to class. This module includes clinically relevant content, active engagement will help you connect basic science to real‑world applications. Regular revision of hormonal pathways and anatomical diagrams is strongly recommended.

learning_activities.topic:
Lecture series - Microbiology by Dr Steven Hancock

BIOM1071- Microbiology Module

Instructor: Dr Steven Hancock

Contact Hours: 4 lectures + 1 revision lecture

Module Overview

In this module, you will be introduced to the fundamental concepts of microbiology, with a focus on the major classes of microorganisms and their relevance to human health. The content is organised into four key areas:

1. Classification and Characteristics of Microorganisms

Identify the key features of the four main microbial groups:

  • Bacteria (prokaryotic structure, reproduction, and diversity)
  • Viruses (structure, replication strategies, and host specificity)
  • Fungi (eukaryotic organisms, including yeasts and moulds)
  • Parasites (protozoa and helminths)
  • Understand the basic biology and life cycles of each group.

2. Medically Relevant Microorganisms and Associated Infections

  • Recognise which microorganisms are clinically significant and why.
  • Learn examples of common bacterial infections (e.g., streptococcal infections, tuberculosis).
  • Learn examples of common viral infections (e.g., influenza, HIV, hepatitis).
  • Learn examples of common fungal and parasitic infections (e.g., candidiasis, malaria).
  • Understand how pathogens cause disease (mechanisms of virulence, transmission routes).

3. Evolution of Infection

  • Explore how microorganisms evolve and adapt to hosts and environments.
  • Understand concepts such as antimicrobial resistance and the emergence of new pathogens.
  • Discuss how evolutionary pressures shape infection outcomes and treatment challenges.

4. Treatment and Control Processes

  • Gain an overview of approaches to managing microbial infections:
  • Antibiotics (bacterial targets, mechanisms of action, and resistance)
  • Antivirals, antifungals, and antiparasitics
  • Infection prevention strategies (vaccination, hygiene, public health measures)
  • Understand the importance of laboratory diagnosis (culture, microscopy, molecular methods) in guiding treatment.

Learning Outcomes

By the end of this module, you should be able to:

  • Describe the basic structure, replication, and classification of bacteria, viruses, fungi, and parasites.
  • Identify medically important microorganisms and the infections they cause.
  • Explain how microorganisms evolve and how this affects disease transmission and treatment.
  • Outline the principles of antimicrobial therapy and infection control.
  • Apply basic microbiological knowledge to understand common clinical scenarios.

Recommended Readings / Resources

Textbook: Refer to the recommended course textbook(s) for detailed reading on each microbial group and infection topics.

Mastering A&P: Use the online platform for supplementary activities, quizzes, and revision tools to reinforce lecture content.

  • Specific chapters and assignments may be advised during lectures- check Blackboard for updates.


Preparation

Review lecture slides and recommended readings before each session. Familiarity with basic cell biology (prokaryotic vs. eukaryotic) will be helpful. Active use of Mastering A&P practice questions is encouraged to test your understanding as you progress through the module.


Learning outcomes: L03, L05, L06, L07, L08

learning_activities.topic:
Lecture series - Immunology by Professor Kate Stacey

BIOM1071- Immunology Module

Lecturer: Professor Kate Stacey

Contact Hours: 5 lectures + 1 revision lecture

Module Overview

In this module, you will explore the fundamental concepts of immunology, including the different types of immunity, their roles in defending the body, and the clinical applications of immunological knowledge. The content is organised into six themed lectures as outlined below.

1. Introduction to Immunology

  • Define immunity and the purpose of the immune system.
  • Identify primary and secondary lymphoid organs (bone marrow, thymus, lymph nodes, spleen).
  • Distinguish between innate immunity (rapid, non‑specific) and acquired immunity (slower, specific, memory‑based).

2. Innate Immunity

  • Describe physical and chemical barriers (skin, mucous membranes, antimicrobial enzymes).
  • Explain the roles of phagocytes (neutrophils, macrophages), natural killer (NK) cells, and dendritic cells.
  • Understand the complement system and the inflammatory response.

3. Acquired (Adaptive) Immunity

  • Detail the functions of B lymphocytes (humoral immunity- antibody production).
  • Detail the functions of T lymphocytes (cell‑mediated immunity- helper and cytotoxic T cells).
  • Explain antigen processing and presentation via MHC class I and II molecules.
  • Describe the generation of immunological memory and the secondary response.

4. Infection Spread and Vaccination

  • Understand routes of pathogen transmission and how infections establish within the body.
  • Explain the rationale behind vaccination and its role in public health.
  • Compare different vaccine platforms and their mechanisms of inducing protective immunity.
  • Discuss the concept of herd immunity and its importance in controlling outbreaks.

5. Immunology in Medicine

  • Explore immunological disorders:
  • Hypersensitivity (allergies, anaphylaxis)
  • Autoimmunity (e.g., type 1 diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis)
  • Immunodeficiency (primary and acquired, e.g., HIV/AIDS)
  • Understand transplant immunology and graft rejection.
  • Introduce immunotherapies, including monoclonal antibodies and checkpoint inhibitors.

6. Revision and Integration

  • Consolidate the connections between innate and acquired immunity.
  • Apply knowledge to clinical case scenarios.
  • Review key definitions, cell types, and signalling pathways.
  • Prepare for assessments with practice questions and concept mapping.

Learning Outcomes

By the end of this module, you should be able to:

  • Distinguish between innate and acquired immunity and explain how they interact.
  • Identify the major immune cells, tissues, and molecules and describe their functions.
  • Explain how vaccines generate protective immunity and why they are critical for public health.
  • Describe common immunological disorders and their underlying mechanisms.
  • Apply immunological principles to interpret clinical cases and treatment strategies.

Recommended Readings / Resources

Textbook: Refer to the recommended course textbook(s) for detailed reading on each immune topic.

Mastering A&P:

  • Use the online platform for interactive quizzes, animations, and revision tools to reinforce lecture content.
  • Specific chapters and assigned activities will be indicated during lectures- check Blackboard for updates.

Preparation

Review lecture slides and associated readings before each session. This module builds progressively from basic concepts to clinical applications – regular revision of earlier material is strongly advised. Active use of Mastering A&P practice questions and participation in revision sessions will enhance your understanding and exam readiness.


Learning outcomes: L03, L04, L06, L07, L08

learning_activities.topic:
BIOM1071- Pre-Examination Revision by Dr Awais Saleem Babri

This dedicated revision session is designed to help you consolidate your learning across all modules and prepare effectively for the final examination. Dr Babri will guide you through a structured review of key concepts from the entire semester, with emphasis on high‑yield topics and commonly assessed areas across the Respiratory, Cardiovascular, Digestive & Renal, Reproduction, Microbiology, and Immunology modules. You will work through exam‑style practice questions, including multiple‑choice, short‑answer, and scenario‑based problems, with discussion of model answers and marking criteria to help you understand what examiners are looking for. The session will also focus on integrating knowledge across body systems, applying physiological and microbiological principles to clinical‑style case scenarios, and strengthening critical thinking skills. Additionally, Dr Babri will provide practical study strategies, including time management tips and active revision techniques, to help you structure your final revision week effectively. Bring your questions and problem areas- this is your opportunity to clarify difficult concepts and build confidence before the exam. Your active participation is strongly encouraged to maximise the benefits of this session.


Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04, L05, L06, L07, L08
